title: Sampling and the central limit theorem
summary: Why sample statistics wobble, how much, and why averages are bell-shaped.

steps.title: Populations and samples
body: You almost never measure everyone. You measure a **sample** and use it to say something about the **population**. A sample statistic (the sample mean, say) is a random quantity: a different sample gives a different answer.
`replace=False` draws distinct members, like surveying 10 different people. `replace=True` allows repeats.

steps.explain: Drawing all 20 without replacement is a shuffle: 20 distinct values that still sum to 210. A population of one value can only ever give that value.

steps.title: The sampling distribution, by simulation
body: How much does the sample mean wobble? Simulate it: draw many samples and look at the spread of their means. One call can draw them all as a 2-D array, one sample per row:
draws = rng.choice(population, size=(1000, 25), replace=True)   # 1000 samples of 25
The standard deviation of the sample means is called the **standard error** (SE). It shrinks as samples grow: `SE = sigma / sqrt(n)`.

steps.prompt: A population has standard deviation 12. What does this print?
steps.explain: Each time n is multiplied by 4, the standard error halves. Precision is expensive: twice as precise needs four times the data.

steps.prompt: You want to halve the standard error of your survey's average. How many more people do you need?
options: It does not depend on the sample size
steps.explain: SE = sigma / sqrt(n). Halving it needs sqrt(n) to double, so n must quadruple.

steps.title: Simulate sample means
prompt: Write `sample_means(pop, n, reps, rng)` returning a NumPy array of `reps` sample means, each from a sample of size `n` drawn **with replacement** from `pop` using the generator `rng`.
Draw everything in one call: `rng.choice(pop, size=(reps, n), replace=True)`, then average each row. No loops.
The tests check the length, that the means centre on the population mean, and that their spread is close to `sigma / sqrt(n)`.
hints: `rng.choice(pop, size=(reps, n), replace=True)` gives a reps x n array.
template: Dojo.check("means centre on the population mean", abs(_m.mean() - _pop.mean()) < 0.2, f"mean of means {_m.mean():.2f}, population {_pop.mean():.2f}")
Dojo.check("spread is close to sigma / sqrt(n)", abs(_m.std() - _se) / _se < 0.08, f"std of means {_m.std():.3f}, expected about {_se:.3f}")

steps.title: The central limit theorem
body: Here is the surprise: even when the population is skewed, the **means** of reasonably large samples form a bell curve centred on the population mean with spread `sigma / sqrt(n)`. That is the **central limit theorem** (CLT).
plt.hist(means, bins=30)                         # a bell, centred near 10
It is why averages, totals and many test statistics behave predictably, and why confidence intervals and A/B tests work.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to plot the sampling distribution of the mean.

steps.title: The CLT experiment
prompt: Write `clt_experiment(pop, sizes, reps, rng)` that, for each sample size `n` in `sizes`, simulates `reps` sample means (with replacement, one `rng.choice` call per size) and records their standard deviation.

Return a dict `{n: standard_error}` with each value a plain float rounded to 3 decimals, and draw a line chart of standard error against sample size: `plt.plot(sizes, ses, marker="o")`, x label `"sample size"`, y label `"standard error"`.
The tests check that the standard error shrinks with `n` and roughly follows `1 / sqrt(n)`.
